requirements.summary: Created /etc/logrotate.d/inventory with a 'daily' stanza; logrotate -d dry-run confirms 'rotating pattern: /var/log/inventory/app.log after 1 days'.
Config specifies 'rotate 7' and 'compress'; forced rotation produced app.log-20260929.gz whose content was verified via zcat to match the pre-rotation log.

requirements.requirement: Application can continue writing to the log after rotation without restart/signal
requirements.summary: copytruncate strategy used; inode of app.log (65543) was identical before and immediately after the forced rotation, and a write issued right after rotation landed successfully in the fresh app.log. Post-reboot write also succeeded, confirming durability of the behavior.

requirements.requirement: Rotation actually runs automatically on a daily cadence (not just configured on paper)
requirements.summary: crond was stopped at discovery; executor enabled it in the default runlevel and started it, confirmed still enabled/started after reboot. /etc/periodic/daily/logrotate (from the logrotate-openrc package) invokes logrotate against /etc/logrotate.conf, which includes /etc/logrotate.d. No literal midnight firing was observed (not practical within the session), but the scheduling mechanism and forced-run behavior were both directly verified.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol executed on node1
requirements.summary: Pre-restart baseline captured (boot_id a7ca5ddf..., crond started, config/log state) at cmd-01a7eba9bdfe4d7a; reboot acknowledged at cmd-a03e4ea2dbe04365; post-restart boot_id (71fabf0a..., uptime 17s) differs at cmd-77790d47ec184020; recovered service/config/data state confirmed at cmd-76d3265a22594553 and cmd-10ae4b9e8b324351. Corroborated by the fixed global boot-identity snapshots (after_prepare a7ca5ddf... -> after_executor 71fabf0a...).

overall_summary: The executor satisfied all material parts of the task: /var/log/inventory/app.log is configured in /etc/logrotate.d/inventory with daily rotation, 7 compressed rotations, and copytruncate so the application keeps writing to the same inode after rotation. A forced rotation directly demonstrated correct compressed-archive creation and uninterrupted writes, and crond (previously stopped) was enabled and started so the daily periodic job actually fires. The independent node-restart evidence protocol was also executed cleanly for node1, showing a healthy pre-restart baseline, an acknowledged reboot, a distinct post-restart boot identity, and full recovery of crond, the logrotate config, the rotated archive, and log writability — corroborated by the fixed global boot-identity snapshots. Hygiene is good but not perfect: verification writes overwrote the live log's original content with test strings, and a small /tmp/reboot.log artifact was left behind.
limitations: No observation of an actual scheduled (midnight) logrotate firing via crond; automatic scheduling is inferred from crond being enabled/started plus the existing /etc/periodic/daily/logrotate hook, not from a real daily execution.

The live app.log content was overwritten with synthetic test strings during verification, so the pre-existing production log content is only recoverable from the rotated .gz archive, not the live file.

operational_hygiene.summary: Most actions were necessary and appropriately scoped: package install, logrotate.d config creation, crond enable/start, dry-run validation, and a bounded forced-rotation test. Two minor residue items remain uncleaned: (1) the forced-rotation and post-reboot verification writes (cmd-ca1186c144f240cd, cmd-10ae4b9e8b324351) replaced the original application log content ('inventory service started...') with synthetic test strings ('pre-rotate write', 'post-rotate write', 'post-reboot write') that were never restored, so the live app.log now only contains test data rather than original application output (original content is preserved only inside the rotated .gz archive); (2) /tmp/reboot.log, created by the backgrounded reboot command (cmd-a03e4ea2dbe04365), was left on disk and shows up as new residue in the after_executor temporary-files snapshot versus after_prepare. Both are low-risk, non-destructive, and plausibly necessary for evidence collection, but neither was cleaned up afterward. No failed/conflicting services, no unsafe exposure changes (only an expected SSH PID/DHCP lease change from the reboot), and package health (apk check) is unchanged from baseline.
